data.text: A **class** is a blueprint. It describes what data an object will hold (attributes) and what it can do (methods). Writing a class does not create anything yet — it only describes it.
An **object** is an *instance* of a class: a real thing in memory with its own values. `Dog("Buddy")` and `Dog("Max")` are two separate objects built from the same `Dog` class.

data.markdown:
Think of an architect's **blueprint** for a house. It is drawn once, but many houses can be built from it.
Every house has the same rooms (same *attributes* and *methods*), yet each one has its own paint colour and owner (its own *values*).

In Python the blueprint is the `class` statement, and each house is an object created by *calling* the class like a function: `Dog("Buddy")`.

data.text: **Encapsulation** means bundling data and the methods that work on it inside one class, and *hiding* the data so it can only be changed through those methods. The class protects its own rules.

data.markdown:
Imagine a bank account where anyone could write `account.balance = -1_000_000`. Nothing would stop invalid values.

With encapsulation the balance is **private**, and the only way to change it is through methods such as `deposit()` and `withdraw()`.
Those methods can check the rules first (*no negative deposits, no overdrafts*).

In Python a double underscore prefix (`self.__balance`) triggers **name mangling**, which makes the attribute hard to reach from outside the class.

rows: Protected by convention ("internal, please don't touch")

data.text: Encapsulation is not about secrecy — it is about **keeping objects valid**. Put the validation inside the methods that change the data.

items: Keep data and the methods that change it together.
Make internal data private (`__name`) and expose methods instead.
Methods like `deposit()` can enforce rules that plain attribute access cannot.
Getters (`get_balance()`) give read access without allowing writes.

data.text: **Inheritance** lets a new class (the *child* or *subclass*) reuse the attributes and methods of an existing class (the *parent* or *base class*). The child can add new behaviour or **override** what it inherited.

data.markdown:
Inheritance models an **is-a** relationship: a `Dog` *is an* `Animal`, a `Car` *is a* `Vehicle`.

```python
class Dog(Animal):   # Dog inherits from Animal
    ...
```

Everything `Animal` defines (`name`, `__init__`, …) is available on a `Dog` for free.
If `Dog` defines a method with the same name as the parent — like `speak()` — the child's version wins. That is called **overriding**.

Check if an object is of a class or its parents

data.text: Only inherit when the *is-a* sentence is true. "A Car **has an** Engine" is composition — store an `Engine` object as an attribute instead of inheriting from it.

items: Children get the parent's attributes and methods for free.
Override a method to change behaviour in the child.
Use `super()` to extend (not replace) the parent's behaviour.
Prefer composition (has-a) when the is-a test fails.

data.text: **Polymorphism** ("many forms") means the *same* method call works on objects of *different* classes, and each object responds in its own way. Code can use `shape.area()` without knowing whether `shape` is a circle or a rectangle.

data.markdown:
A TV remote has one **power** button, yet it works on every brand of TV. You don't care *how* each TV turns on — you just press the button.

In code:

```python
for shape in [Circle(5), Rectangle(4, 6)]:
    print(shape.area())      # the right area() is chosen automatically
```

The loop never checks the type. Adding a `Triangle` later needs **no change** to the loop — only a new class with an `area()` method.

rows: High — easy to miss a branch

data.text: Python uses **duck typing**: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck". Objects don't even need a common parent — they just need the method.

items: Same method name, different behaviour per class.
Callers depend on the method, not the concrete type.
New types can be added without changing existing code.

data.text: **Abstraction** means exposing *what* an object does while hiding *how* it does it. An **abstract class** defines methods that subclasses must implement, and cannot be instantiated itself.

data.markdown:
To drive you only need the steering wheel, pedals and gear stick — the **interface**. You don't need to know how fuel injection works.

In Python, `abc.ABC` and `@abstractmethod` let you write that interface:

```python
class Payment(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def pay(self, amount): ...
```

Every concrete payment type (credit card, PayPal, …) must implement `pay()`. Code that takes payments only talks to `Payment`.

data.text: If a subclass forgets to implement even one abstract method, Python refuses to create it: *TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ... with abstract method pay*.

items: Abstraction hides implementation details behind a simple interface.
Use `ABC` + `@abstractmethod` to define a contract.
Abstract classes can't be instantiated; subclasses must fill in the gaps.

data.text: A class should have **one, and only one, reason to change**. Each class focuses on a single job, so a change in one concern (e.g. how a report is printed) doesn't touch unrelated code (how the report data is built).

data.markdown:
Ask: *"Who would ask me to change this class?"* If the answer is several different people — the accountant **and** the designer **and** the DBA — the class has several responsibilities.

A quick smell test is the word **"and"** in a description: *"This class calculates totals **and** saves them **and** emails them."*

Splitting responsibilities gives smaller classes that are easier to read, test and reuse.

data.text: Software entities should be **open for extension** but **closed for modification**. You add new behaviour by writing *new* code (e.g. a new class), not by editing code that already works.

data.markdown:
Think of a power strip: you add a new device by **plugging it in**, not by rewiring the strip.

The usual technique is an **abstraction** (an abstract class or interface). Existing code depends on the abstraction; new behaviour arrives as a new subclass.

```python
def checkout(price, discount: Discount):   # closed — never edited again
    return discount.apply(price)

class StudentDiscount(Discount):            # open — new behaviour plugs in
    def apply(self, price): return price * 0.8
```

data.text: Objects of a subclass must be usable **anywhere** an object of the parent class is expected, **without breaking** the program. A subclass may extend behaviour, but must not break the promises its parent makes.

data.markdown:
If `Bird` promises `fly()`, then *every* bird subclass must be able to fly. A `Penguin` that raises an exception in `fly()` breaks that promise — any code looping over birds and calling `fly()` will crash.

The fix is to model the hierarchy so that promises are only made where they're true:

- `Bird` → things **all** birds do (`eat()`)
- `FlyingBird(Bird)` → adds `fly()`
- `Penguin(Bird)` → never promised to fly

data.text: **No class should be forced to implement methods it does not use.** Prefer several small, focused interfaces over one large "fat" interface.

data.markdown:
Imagine a `Worker` interface with `work()`, `eat()` and `sleep()`. A `Robot` can work but doesn't eat or sleep — yet it's forced to implement those methods, usually with `raise NotImplementedError` (which then breaks LSP too).

Splitting the interface fixes it:

- `Workable` → `work()`
- `Eatable` → `eat()`

A `Human` implements both; a `Robot` implements only `Workable`. In Python a class can inherit from several ABCs at once.

rows: Only the classes that need it
Clients see methods they never call
Clients see only what they use
A class should have one reason to change
Extend behaviour without editing existing code
Subclasses must work wherever the parent works
Many small interfaces beat one fat interface
Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes

data.text: If you find yourself writing `raise NotImplementedError` in a subclass just to satisfy an interface, the interface is probably too big.

items: Small, role-based interfaces beat one big interface.

data.text: **High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.** Business logic (like placing an order) talks to an interface (`Notifier`), not to a specific technology (`EmailNotifier`).

data.markdown:
A lamp doesn't care which power station produced the electricity — it only depends on the **socket** (the abstraction). You can switch to solar without rewiring the lamp.

In code, the abstraction is usually passed in from outside — **dependency injection**:

```python
class Order:
    def __init__(self, notifier: Notifier):   # injected
        self.notifier = notifier
```

Now `Order` works with email, SMS, push — or a fake notifier in tests.

rows: A class should have one reason to change
Extend behaviour without editing existing code
Subclasses must work wherever the parent works
Many small interfaces beat one fat interface
Depend on abstractions, not concrete classes

data.text: Dependency *Inversion* is the principle; dependency *Injection* (passing collaborators in through the constructor) is the most common way to apply it.

items: Business logic depends on abstractions, not implementations.
Pass dependencies in (dependency injection) instead of creating them inside.
Swapping implementations — or using fakes in tests — becomes trivial.

data.text: The **Singleton** pattern ensures a class has **only one instance** and provides a single, global point of access to it. Every call to the constructor returns the *same* object.

data.markdown:
Some things should exist exactly once in a program: the application's **configuration**, a **connection pool**, a **logger**.
If two parts of the code each created their own `Config`, a setting changed in one place wouldn't be seen in the other.

In Python the simplest way is to override `__new__`, which runs *before* `__init__` and decides which object to return:
if an instance already exists, return it instead of creating a new one.

rows: Lazy creation — made only when first needed

data.text: Use Singleton sparingly. Passing a shared object in explicitly (dependency injection) is often clearer and easier to test.

items: One class → one instance, shared everywhere.
In Python, override `__new__` to return the stored instance.
Great for config and shared resources; overusing it creates hidden global state.

data.caption: The class stores its only instance in a class-level attribute.

data.plantUml:
@startuml
participant "c1 = Config()" as A
participant "c2 = Config()" as B
participant "Config" as C
A -> C : __new__()
C -> C : _instance is None → create
C --> A : instance #1
B -> C : __new__()
C -> C : _instance exists
C --> B : same instance #1
@enduml
data.caption: The second call gets the object created by the first.

steps.explanation: `__new__` runs again, but `_instance` is already set, so it returns the existing object.

data.text: The **Factory** pattern moves object creation into a dedicated method or class. Callers ask the factory for *"a car"* and get back the right object, without calling constructors or knowing concrete class names.

data.markdown:
You order *"pasta"* from the menu; the kitchen decides which chef, pan and recipe to use. You never walk into the kitchen.

A factory works the same way:

```python
vehicle = VehicleFactory.create("car")   # which class? the factory decides
vehicle.drive()
```

When you add a `Truck`, only the factory changes — not the dozens of places that create vehicles.

rows: Choose type from config / user input

data.text: Factories pair well with polymorphism: every product shares an interface (here `drive()`), so callers don't care which one they got.

items: Centralise creation logic in one place.
Callers depend on the product interface, not concrete classes.
Invalid requests can be rejected in one spot (e.g. ValueError).

data.text: The **Observer** pattern defines a **one-to-many** relationship: when one object (the *subject* or *publisher*) changes or emits an event, all its registered *observers* (subscribers) are notified automatically.

rows: Keeps a list of observers and notifies them

data.text: GUI buttons (`on_click`), event buses and spreadsheet cells that update when others change are all Observer in action.

items: The subject doesn't know what observers do — loose coupling.
Observers can be added or removed at runtime.
Only observers subscribed *before* an event receive it.

data.text: The **Strategy** pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms, puts each in its own class, and lets the client (the *context*) choose one at runtime — without changing the context's code.

data.markdown:
You can drive, take a bus or call a taxi. The *goal* is the same; the *strategy* differs, and you can switch based on time or budget.

In code, the **context** (`Sorter`) holds a reference to a strategy object and delegates the work to it:

```python
sorter = Sorter(BubbleSort())
sorter.sort(data)            # uses bubble sort
sorter.strategy = BuiltinSort()
sorter.sort(data)            # same Sorter, different algorithm
```

data.text: Strategy is the Open/Closed Principle applied to algorithms: the context is closed for modification, the set of strategies is open for extension.

items: Each algorithm lives in its own class with a shared interface.
The context delegates to whatever strategy it holds.
Strategies can be swapped at runtime.

data.text: The **Decorator** pattern adds responsibilities to an object **dynamically** by wrapping it in another object that has the **same interface**. Wrappers can be stacked, each adding a little behaviour.

data.markdown:
Start with a plain coffee. Add milk: it's still a coffee, just more expensive. Add sugar on top: still a coffee.

Each add-on **wraps** the previous drink and forwards calls to it, adding its own bit:

```python
order = SugarDecorator(MilkDecorator(Coffee()))
order.cost()   # 5 + 2 + 1 = 8
```

Without decorators you'd need a subclass for every combination — `CoffeeWithMilk`, `CoffeeWithSugar`, `CoffeeWithMilkAndSugar`, …

data.text: Python's `@decorator` syntax for functions is related but not identical: it wraps *functions*, while the Decorator pattern wraps *objects*. The idea — wrap and extend — is the same.

items: A decorator has the same interface as the object it wraps.
It forwards calls to the wrapped object and adds behaviour.
Decorators stack to build combinations at runtime.

data.caption: Each decorator is a Beverage that wraps another Beverage.

data.plantUml:
@startuml
object "SugarDecorator" as S
object "MilkDecorator" as M
object "Coffee" as C
S *-- M : wraps
M *-- C : wraps
note right of S : cost() = M.cost() + 1
note right of M : cost() = C.cost() + 2
note right of C : cost() = 5
@enduml
data.caption: Calls travel inward, and each layer adds to the result on the way out.
